title: Manchester United experienced despair against Leeds. What matters most is what happens next
content:
Manchester United returned from a three-week footballing hibernation, working within an (injury-related) uneven structure, a few players short of their strongest XI. They ran into a clenched fist and were unsure how best to fight back.

Monday night’s meeting with Leeds United was the sort of potential banana skin that makes many a football manager take pause. At home against a rival who relish playing as the underdog and were eager to earn some separation between themselves and the relegation zone, Leeds’ travelling fans fed into a bear-pit atmosphere at Old Trafford.

Leeds wanted to play fast and try to take United by surprise. United wanted to play at their own pace and defang the volatile emotional element of this old rivalry, but, following a 23-day pause in Premier League football, they played too slowly and allowed ring rust to set in.

Carrick’s players found themselves caught cold by Leeds’ aggression and intensity in the first half. They battled bravely for the game’s final 30 minutes after being reduced to 10 men following Lisandro Martinez’s red card for clawing at Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s hair, but fell to a 2-1 defeat that will go down in Leeds folklore, the visitors winning their first league game at Old Trafford since 1981.

For Carrick, it is the first home defeat of his interim period and his United team have only experienced one win in their last four matches. They have gone five games without earning a clean sheet, and have suffered two red cards in their last two fixtures.

Squad depth is an issue, as are player injuries, but the combative, confident and hyper-skilled performances of January and February have given way to something more passive and workmanlike. Results elsewhere in the race for the top five mean this loss is not a total disaster, but United can ill-afford another lethargic display in any of their remaining six games of the season.

How they perform between now and the end of 2025-26 matters almost as much as how quickly they can earn a much-desired place in next season’s Champions League. Carrick won’t want his team to crawl over the finish line, but he’ll need to make some adjustments to help them better gut out the race’s final miles.

Why were United so unprepared for Leeds? The prolonged break since their 2-2 draw against Bournemouth did not help, nor did a duo of enforced changes to the starting XI.

An injury to Kobbie Mainoo saw Manuel Ugarte given his first start under Carrick, and the defensive midfielder spent the majority of the match chasing shadows. Harry Maguire’s red card from the draw against Bournemouth saw Carrick pair Martinez with Leny Yoro at centre-back, and neither man looked comfortable facing wave after wave of attacking pressure.

United were slow to react to a much more physical opponent, and Daniel Farke sent his players to Old Trafford to hunt for the ball in packs and attack United’s most vulnerable players on their outside shoulder. It limited the usefulness of Casemiro, Matheus Cunha and others whenever they came onto the ball. They were rarely afforded the time to take a second touch.

Two first-half goals from Noah Okafor put the visitors in command of things, while Carrick’s men struggled to construct any settled periods of possession. United approached the first half thinking it was similar to a gentleman’s duel. Leeds turned up to Old Trafford looking for a street fight.

Carrick’s men struggled to settle or play with their usual authority and Bruno Fernandes tried his best to alleviate his team’s most troubling concerns, but there are only so many times the club captain can drop deep to collect the ball before it creates a vacuum in the spaces ahead.

Things were made more complicated early in the second half when Martinez was shown a straight red card early in the second half after a VAR review for pulling Calvert-Lewin’s hair. Leeds’ dominance was at such a level across an hour that fans in the away section were offering “ole!” chants on every completed pass. A goal from Casemiro, scored eight minutes later, put an end to such celebrations and began a momentum swing that did not create enough to avoid defeat, but would at least give Carrick and his coaching staff some food for thought.

Manchester United waited 23 days to play another Premier League game after the Bournemouth draw that saw one of their centre-backs sent off and added another pothole to an already craggy road to Champions League qualification. This 2-1 defeat to Leeds brings another red card and strains a squad ill-equipped for further stress-testing. (Carrick vehemently disagreed with the decision but Martinez will receive a three-game suspension unless United successfully appeal the red card and have it overturned.)

Yet United remain third in the league table and masters of their own fate in their race for European qualification. Confidence will be dented but not derailed, and Saturday’s fixture against Chelsea gives Carrick the chance for a quick reset.

United’s approach when out of possession needs refinement, with the coaching staff ideally wanting to restore the compact 4-4-2 seen in victories over Manchester City and Arsenal, and greater intensity when looking to regain possession.

Yoro will have to use Monday’s duels with Calvert-Lewin as a learning curve. The 20-year-old is a promising centre-back, but his team will need him to better impose themselves on matches for the remainder of this season and the ones to come after. Fernandes remains a supreme creator, and his ability to find Casemiro in the air gives the team a goalscoring threat, but others around them need to find more consistency.

United, a team that can stumble and soar in equal measure, have found ways to limit the former to smaller spurts and now need to extend their sunnier periods.

It can be done. It will be difficult, but Champions League football is likely to be achieved before the end of the season. The challenge for Carrick and his staff will be to finish 2025-26 convincingly and create a positive environment for whoever takes over permanently after that — be that the current United head coach himself or someone else.

The Premier League table does not afford additional points for style, but the manner in which United secure European qualification will influence the hearts and minds of fans for the summer ahead.
